```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(

pkgs <- c("khroma", "viridisLite", "RColorBrewer", "patchwork", "ggplot2", "DT", "htmltools")
to_install <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(to_install) > 0L) install.packages(to_install)

show_colors_html <- function(colors, height = "25px") {
  div_tags <- lapply(colors, function(color) {
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = paste("background-color:", color, ";",
                    "width: 100%; height:", height, ";",
                    "display: inline-block;")
    )
  })
  htmltools::tagList(htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "display: flex; width: 100%;", div_tags
  ))
}
```

# Why `colortheme`?

R has a rich ecosystem of color palettes—across **grDevices**, **RColorBrewer**, **viridisLite**, **khroma**, and more. Yet, applying and customizing colors in daily data analysis or package development still involves unnecessary friction:

1. **Function Explosion in `ggplot2`**: Switching between palette sources or scale types requires rewriting the function call itself—jumping between `scale_color_brewer()`, `scale_color_viridis_d()`, `scale_color_viridis_c()`, `scale_color_gradient2()`, and `scale_color_stepsn()`. Even reversing a palette changes from `direction = -1` to `rev = TRUE` depending on the function.
2. **Static Aggregators & Heavy Dependencies**: Meta-packages like **paletteer** are fantastic dictionaries for discovering palettes, but they carry a heavy dependency footprint and treat palettes mainly as static color vectors. Expressing dynamic behavior—such as *highlighting specific categories while graying out the rest*, or *quantizing a continuous gradient with a neutral dead-zone*—still requires manual data wrangling or custom scale functions.
3. **The Base R vs. `ggplot2` Divide**: `ggplot2` scales cannot be used in Base R `plot()` or `image()`, forcing analysts and package authors to manually write rescaling, midpoint alignment, and `NA`-handling logic whenever they step outside `ggplot2`.

**`colortheme`** solves these problems not by collecting thousands of static vectors, but by encapsulating **color behavior** into a lightweight, zero-dependency S3 object and a **compact URL-like query syntax**:

```r
# Traditional approach: different functions, different arguments, manual data prep
scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, alpha = 0.8)
scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "RdBu", breaks = c(0.2, 0.8))

# With colortheme: one function, expressive query strings
scale_fill_theme("mako_r?alpha=0.8")
scale_fill_theme("RdBu?ramp.steps=c(0.2, 0.8)")
scale_fill_theme("highlight?which=list(1:2, -1)")
```

---

# 1. Expressive Plotting with **ggplot2**

With `scale_color_theme()` and `scale_fill_theme()`, you never have to switch scale functions again. Everything—source selection, reversal (`_r`), type casting (`@qual`, `@seq`, `@div`), category highlighting, and step quantization (`?ramp.steps=...`)—is controlled through a single string.

### Programmable Highlighting & Discrete Scales

Instead of mutating your data frame to create a `"target vs. others"` column, use the built-in `"highlight"` theme directly in the scale query. You can pass negative indices (e.g., `-1` for the last category) or `list()` objects to group multiple categories under the same accent color. Setting `base = 'transparent'` (or `NA`) visually hides non-target points.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.2, warning = FALSE}
library(colortheme)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))

set.seed(42)
dataset <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 5000L), ]

p <- ggplot(dataset) + geom_point(aes(carat, price, col = color), size = 1.2)
p + scale_color_theme("shiki") +
  ggtitle('"shiki" (Built-in Japanese palette)')
p + scale_color_theme("viridisLite/mako@qual") +
  ggtitle('"viridisLite/mako@qual" (cast to Qualitative)')
p + scale_color_theme("highlight?which=list(1:2, -1)") +
  ggtitle('"highlight?which=list(1:2, -1)"')
p + scale_color_theme("highlight?base='transparent'&which=c(1, 7)") +
  ggtitle('"highlight?base=\'transparent\'&which=c(1, 7)"')
```

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.2, warning = FALSE}
p2 <- ggplot(dataset) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = carat, fill = cut), bins = 20)
p2 + scale_fill_theme("ukiyoe") +
  ggtitle('"ukiyoe"')
p2 + scale_fill_theme("highlight_r?which=list(1:2, 5)") +
  ggtitle('"highlight_r?which=list(1:2, 5)"')
p2 + scale_fill_theme("ai@q") +
  ggtitle('"ai@q" (cast to Qualitative)')
p2 + scale_fill_theme("Zissou 1_r@q") +
  ggtitle('"Zissou 1_r@q"')
```

### Continuous, Diverging, and Stepped Scales

For continuous variables, diverging themes automatically align their center color to `middle` (default `0`) via `scales::rescale_mid()`. Furthermore, adding `?ramp.steps=k` (for $k$ equal bins) or `?ramp.steps=c(...)` (for custom cutoffs in $(0, 1)$) converts *any* continuous theme into a stepped (binned) scale on the fly.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.2, warning = FALSE}
p3 <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster()
p3 + scale_fill_theme("ai") +
  ggtitle('"ai"')
p3 + scale_fill_theme("Cividis", middle = 0.02) +
  ggtitle('"Cividis"')
p3 + scale_fill_theme("steps", middle = 0.02) +
  ggtitle('"steps"')
p3 + scale_fill_theme("magma?ramp.steps=11&alpha=0.8") +
  ggtitle('"magma?ramp.steps=9&alpha=0.8"')
```

---

# 2. The Query Syntax & Core Mechanics

Every `"colortheme"` object encapsulates two color-generating functions:

- **`$palette(n)`**: Accepts an integer $n$ and returns $n$ discrete colors (recycling or interpolating as configured).
- **`$ramp(x)`**: Accepts a numeric vector $x \in [0, 1]$ and maps it onto a continuous or stepped color gradient.

```{r, fig.height = 1.2, fig.width = 6, warning = FALSE}
azurerose <- colortheme("azurerose")
print(azurerose)
```

You can call `$palette()` and `$ramp()` directly, or extract standalone functions via `as_palette()` and `as_ramp()`:

```{r, fig.height = 0.35, fig.width = 6, echo = c(-2, -4)}
azurerose$palette(5)
# as_palette(azurerose)(5)
show_colors_html(azurerose$palette(5))
azurerose$ramp(seq.int(0, 1, by = 0.1))
# as_ramp(azurerose)(seq.int(0, 1, by = 0.1))
show_colors_html(azurerose$ramp(seq.int(0, 1, by = 0.1)))
```

### Compact Query Grammar: `source/name_r@type?key=value`

Instead of nested function calls, you can modify any theme using a single string:

1. **Prefix (`source/`)**: Disambiguate themes with identical names across packages (e.g., `"RColorBrewer/Paired"` vs. `"grDevices/Paired"`).
2. **Reversal (`_r`)**: Append `_r` to the theme name to reverse the color order.
3. **Type Casting (`@seq`, `@div`, `@qual`)**: Convert a sequential theme into a qualitative palette (which also turns its `$ramp()` into a stepped ramp by default) or vice versa.
4. **Query Parameters (`?k1=v1;k2=v2` or `&`)**: Pass kernel arguments (`alpha`, `begin`, `end`, `which`) or theme options (`ramp.steps`, `na.color`, `kernel.size`) as R expressions.

```{r, fig.height = 1.2, fig.width = 6}
# Equivalent ways to customize a theme: via arguments vs. query syntax
colortheme("viridis", type = "qualitative", kernel.size = 7, begin = 0, end = 1)
colortheme("viridis@qual?kernel.size=7;begin=0;end=1")
```

```{r, fig.height = 1.2, fig.width = 6}
# Quantize into 11 equal steps, or split at custom cutoffs
colortheme("azurerose?ramp.steps=11")
colortheme("azurerose?ramp.steps=seq.int(.4, .6, by = .02)")
```

---

# 3. Direct Data Mapping for Base R & Package Developers

If you use Base R graphics, or if you are developing an R package that provides plotting methods, `map_to_colors()` gives you the same power without requiring **ggplot2**.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
par(mfrow = c(1L, 2L), mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
# Sequential mapping
plot(cars, col = map_to_colors(cars$speed), pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
plot(cars, col = map_to_colors(cars$speed, "ukiyoe"), pch = 19, cex = 1.2)

# Discrete highlighting in Base R
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, pch = 19,
     col = map_to_colors(iris$Species, "highlight?which=1"))
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, pch = 19,
     col = map_to_colors(iris$Species, "highlight_r?which=-1"))
```

### Creating & Registering Custom Themes

You can also construct a `"colortheme"` from any hex vector or palette function, register it into the session via `register_colortheme()`, and set package-wide defaults via `colortheme_options()`.

```{r, fig.height = 1.2, fig.width = 6}
mytheme <- colortheme(
  c("#003f5c", "#7a5195", "#ef5675", "#ffa600"),
  type = "sequential", name = "mytheme"
)
register_colortheme(mytheme, name = "mytheme", source = "custom")
colortheme("custom/mytheme")
colortheme("custom/mytheme_r@q?alpha=0.8")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
remove("mytheme", envir = getOption("colortheme.registry"))
.df <- colorthemes()
```

---

# 4. Pre-defined Color Themes Gallery

The following color themes are available when **colortheme** is loaded (themes from **viridisLite**, **RColorBrewer**, and **khroma** are lazily enabled when those packages are installed).

```{r table, echo = FALSE}
DT::datatable(
  .df,
  class = 'cell-border stripe hover',
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    lengthMenu = c(10, 20, 50, 100),
    dom = 'Btip'
  )
)
```

## Sequential Color Themes

```{r sequential_gallery, echo = FALSE}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
df <- .df[.df$type == "sequential", ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
  ct <- colortheme(df[i, 1L], source = df[i, 2L])
  text <- sprintf("%s/%s", df[i, 2L], df[i, 1L])
  plot(ct, text = text)
}
par(op)
```

## Diverging Color Themes

```{r diverging_gallery, echo = FALSE}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
df <- .df[.df$type == "diverging", ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
  ct <- colortheme(df[i, 1L], source = df[i, 2L])
  text <- sprintf("%s/%s", df[i, 2L], df[i, 1L])
  plot(ct, text = text)
}
par(op)
```

## Qualitative Color Themes

```{r qualitative_gallery, echo = FALSE}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
df <- .df[.df$type == "qualitative", ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
  ct <- colortheme(df[i, 1L], source = df[i, 2L])
  text <- sprintf("%s/%s", df[i, 2L], df[i, 1L])
  plot(ct, text = text)
}
par(op)
```
